title: Vom klugen Schneiderlein
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 114. Text from Wikisource („Vom klugen Schneiderlein (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 114 (Vom klugen Schneiderlein) turns on a proud princess who has already sent every failed suitor away with mockery, and now offers herself as the prize to whoever can guess the two colours of hair on her head. Where two boastful tailors guess wrong, a scorned 'useless' third gets it at once — silver and gold — and when the princess tries to wriggle out of the bargain by shutting him overnight in a stable with a bear, he tricks the animal into breaking its teeth on cobblestones disguised as nuts, then offers to teach it the fiddle and traps its claws fast in a vice under pretence of the lesson. He survives the night unmarked, and the princess, cornered by her own wager, is married to him whether she likes it or not. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as daß, gieng, fieng, ward, Räthsel and thun.

sentences.t: Es war einmal eine Prinzessin gewaltig stolz:
sentences.l: There was once a princess mightily proud:
sentences.i: Once there was a princess who was tremendously proud:
sentences.n: Es war einmal is the fixed opening of a German tale — literally “it was once.” gewaltig stolz is hung on after the noun the way an afterthought is added in speech, and the colon that follows introduces the proof of it.

sentences.t: kam ein Freier, so gab sie ihm etwas zu rathen auf, und wenn ers nicht errathen konnte, so ward er mit Spott fortgeschickt.
sentences.l: came a suitor, then she set him something to guess, and if he could not guess it, then he was sent off with mockery.
sentences.i: if a suitor came, she would set him something to puzzle out, and if he could not puzzle it out, he was sent off with mockery.
sentences.n: A conditional without wenn: kam ein Freier, verb first, means “if a suitor came,” and the so that follows answers it. aufgeben is separable, and the particle auf waits at the end — gab … auf, “set … as a task.” rathen and errathen are the 1857 spellings of raten and erraten; ward is the old past of werden.

sentences.t: Sie ließ auch bekannt machen, wer ihr Räthsel löste, sollte sich mit ihr vermählen, und möchte kommen wer da wollte.
sentences.l: She also had it made known, whoever solved her riddle should wed with her, and might come whoever wanted.
sentences.i: She also had it proclaimed that whoever solved her riddle should marry her, and that any who liked might come.
sentences.n: lassen with an infinitive is the German causative: ließ bekannt machen, “had it made known.” Räthsel is the 1857 spelling of Rätsel. The closing clause is an old turn — möchte kommen wer da wollte, “let come who would” — the subjunctive standing for a general leave granted.

sentences.t: Endlich fanden sich auch drei Schneider zusammen,
sentences.l: At last three tailors also found themselves together,
sentences.i: At last three tailors too came together,
sentences.n: sich zusammenfinden — literally “to find one another together” — is a separable verb used reflexively, and its particle zusammen closes the clause.

sentences.t: davon meinten die zwei ältesten sie hätten so manchen feinen Stich gethan und hättens getroffen, da könnts ihnen nicht fehlen, sie müßtens auch hier treffen;
sentences.l: of them the two eldest thought they had done many a fine stitch and had hit it, there it could not fail them, they would have to hit it here too;
sentences.i: of these the two eldest reckoned that they had made many a fine stitch and had always hit the mark, so it could not fail them here — they were bound to hit it this time as well;
sentences.n: The whole report stands in the subjunctive of reported speech (hätten, könnts, müßtens): the tale is giving their opinion, not its own. Stich is the tailors’ own word, a stitch, and treffen, “to hit,” runs through the tale as the word for guessing right. hättens, könnts and müßtens are the spoken contractions of hätten es, könnte es and müßten es.

sentences.t: der dritte war ein kleiner unnützer Springinsfeld, der nicht einmal sein Handwerk verstand, aber meinte er müßte dabei Glück haben, denn woher sollts ihm sonst kommen.
sentences.l: the third was a little useless spring-into-the-field, who did not even understand his trade, but thought he must have luck at it, for where else should it come to him from.
sentences.i: the third was a useless little scapegrace who did not even know his own trade, but thought that luck must fall to him here, for where else was it to come from.
sentences.n: Springinsfeld is built out of a whole phrase — “spring into the field” — and is a name for a heedless young scamp; the literal keeps the compound visible. unnütz is “of no use.” sollts is sollte es, and the closing words are a question in shape but a shrug in force, which is why the 1857 text ends them with a full stop.

sentences.t: Da sprachen die zwei andern zu ihm „bleib nur zu Haus, du wirst mit deinem bischen Verstande nicht weit kommen.“
sentences.l: Then the two others spoke to him “just stay at home, you will with your bit of understanding not come far.”
sentences.i: Then the two others said to him, “stay at home, why don’t you; you will not get far with the little sense you have.”
sentences.n: sprach (here sprachen) is the tales’ verb for speaking, weightier than sagen; you will meet it on nearly every page. nur softens the imperative into “do just —.” bischen is the 1857 spelling of bißchen, and Verstande carries the old dative -e that has since fallen away.

sentences.t: Das Schneiderlein ließ sich aber nicht irre machen und sagte es hätte einmal seinen Kopf darauf gesetzt und wollte sich schon helfen, und gieng dahin als wäre die ganze Welt sein.
sentences.l: The little tailor, however, did not let itself be made confused and said it had once set its head upon it and would help itself well enough, and went along as if the whole world were his.
sentences.i: But the little tailor would not be put off, and said that he had once set his head on the thing and would manage well enough; and off he went as though the whole world were his.
sentences.n: Schneiderlein is the diminutive of Schneider, and every German diminutive is neuter, so the tale says es and the literal must say “it” where English wants “he.” sich irre machen lassen is “to let oneself be thrown off.” schon here is not “already” but the reassuring “right enough.” gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging.

sentences.t: Da meldeten sich alle drei bei der Prinzessin und sagten sie sollte ihnen ihre Räthsel vorlegen:
sentences.l: Then all three announced themselves to the princess and said she should lay her riddles before them:
sentences.i: Then all three presented themselves to the princess and said she should put her riddles to them:
sentences.n: sich melden bei jemandem is the set phrase for reporting to someone. vorlegen, “to lay before,” is separable, and the reported wish keeps the subjunctive sollte.

sentences.t: es wären die rechten Leute angekommen, die hätten einen feinen Verstand, daß man ihn wohl in eine Nadel fädeln könnte.
sentences.l: the right people had arrived, they had an understanding so fine that one could well thread it into a needle.
sentences.i: the right men had arrived; their wits were so fine that one might thread them through a needle.
sentences.n: Still reported speech, hence wären, hätten, könnte. The boast is a tailors’ joke: fein means both subtle and thin, so an understanding fine enough goes through the eye of a needle, and fädeln belongs to the same trade.

sentences.t: Da sprach die Prinzessin „ich habe zweierlei Haar auf dem Kopf, von was für Farben ist das?“
sentences.l: Then the princess spoke “I have two kinds of hair on my head, of what colours is that?”
sentences.i: Then the princess said, “I have two kinds of hair on my head — what colours are they?”
sentences.n: zweierlei never changes its ending: “of two sorts.” Haar stands in the singular where English wants a plural. von was für Farben is the spoken form of the question; the written language would rather say welcher Farbe.

sentences.t: „Wenns weiter nichts ist,“ sagte der erste, „es wird schwarz und weiß sein, wie Tuch, das man Kümmel und Salz nennt.“
sentences.l: “If it is nothing further,” said the first, “it will be black and white, like cloth that one calls caraway and salt.”
sentences.i: “If that is all,” said the first, “it will be black and white, like the cloth they call caraway-and-salt.”
sentences.n: Wenns is wenn es. Kümmel und Salz — caraway and salt — is the old trade name for a speckled black-and-white cloth; the English name for the same weave is pepper-and-salt. wird … sein is not a future but a guess: “it will be” in the sense of “it must be.”

sentences.t: Die Prinzessin sprach „falsch gerathen, antworte der zweite.“
sentences.l: The princess spoke “wrongly guessed, let the second answer.”
sentences.i: The princess said, “guessed wrong — the second may answer.”
sentences.n: gerathen (modern geraten) is the past participle of rathen, to guess; falsch gerathen is a verdict in two words, with no verb of being. antworte is an imperative addressed to the second tailor.

sentences.t: Da sagte der zweite „ists nicht schwarz und weiß, so ists braun und roth, wie meines Herrn Vaters Bratenrock.“
sentences.l: Then the second said “if it is not black and white, then it is brown and red, like my lord father’s roast-coat.”
sentences.i: Then the second said, “if it is not black and white, then it is brown and red, like my lord father’s Sunday coat.”
sentences.n: ists is ist es, and the verb-first clause is again a conditional with no wenn. Bratenrock — “roast-coat” — is the good coat kept for feast days, when there was roast on the table. meines Herrn Vaters is a genitive piled on a genitive, “my lord father’s.” roth is the 1857 spelling of rot.

sentences.t: „Falsch gerathen,“ sagte die Prinzessin, „antworte der dritte, dem seh ichs an, der weiß es sicherlich.“
sentences.l: “Wrongly guessed,” said the princess, “let the third answer, I see it on him, he knows it certainly.”
sentences.i: “Guessed wrong,” said the princess, “let the third answer; I can see it in his face — he knows it for certain.”
sentences.n: jemandem etwas ansehen is to see a thing in a person’s look, and the particle an stands at the end: seh ichs … an. dem and der are demonstratives here — “that one” — not relative pronouns. weiß in this line is the verb wissen, “knows,” and not the colour of the two lines before.

sentences.t: Da trat das Schneiderlein keck hervor, und sprach „die Prinzessin hat ein silbernes und ein goldenes Haar auf dem Kopf, und das sind die zweierlei Farben.“
sentences.l: Then the little tailor stepped boldly forth, and spoke “the princess has a silver and a golden hair on her head, and those are the two kinds of colours.”
sentences.i: Then the little tailor stepped up boldly and said, “the princess has one silver hair and one golden hair on her head, and those are the two colours.”
sentences.n: hervortreten, “to step forth,” is separable, and hervor waits for the end of the clause. auf dem Kopf carries no possessive: German leaves the owner to be understood where English must say “her head.”

sentences.t: Wie die Prinzessin das hörte, ward sie blaß, und wäre vor Schrecken beinah hingefallen,
sentences.l: When the princess heard that, she grew pale, and would from fright almost have fallen down,
sentences.i: When the princess heard that, she turned pale and would almost have fallen down with fright,
sentences.n: wie means “when,” not “how” — constant in the tales. ward is the old past of werden, here “became.” vor with the dative names the cause of a feeling: vor Schrecken, “out of fright.”

sentences.t: denn das Schneiderlein hatte es getroffen, und sie hatte fest geglaubt das würde kein Mensch auf der Welt heraus bringen.
sentences.l: for the little tailor had hit it, and she had firmly believed no person in the world would bring that out.
sentences.i: for the little tailor had hit the mark, and she had firmly believed that not a soul in the world would find it out.
sentences.n: treffen again for guessing right. herausbringen is “to bring out,” that is, to find out; the 1857 text writes the two halves apart, heraus bringen. kein Mensch is the ordinary German for “nobody.”

sentences.t: Als ihr das Herz wieder kam, sprach sie „damit hast du mich noch nicht gewonnen, du mußt noch eins thun, unten im Stall liegt ein Bär, bei dem sollst du die Nacht zubringen;
sentences.l: When the heart came back to her, she spoke “with that you have not yet won me, you must do one thing more, down in the stable lies a bear, with him you shall pass the night;
sentences.i: When her heart came back to her, she said, “you have not won me with that yet; you must do one thing more. Down in the stable lies a bear, and with him you shall pass the night;
sentences.n: ihr das Herz kam is the dative of the person concerned, where English uses a possessive: “her heart.” thun is the 1857 spelling of tun. zubringen, “to spend, pass” of time, is separable, and sollst here is not moral duty but the condition she lays down.

sentences.t: wenn ich dann morgen aufstehe, und du bist noch lebendig, so sollst du mich heirathen.“
sentences.l: when I then get up tomorrow, and you are still alive, then you shall marry me.”
sentences.i: if I get up tomorrow and you are still alive, then you shall marry me.”
sentences.n: wenn does duty for both “when” and “if.” aufstehen is separable, the auf falling to the end. heirathen is the 1857 spelling of heiraten.

sentences.t: Sie dachte aber damit wollte sie das Schneiderlein los werden, denn der Bär hatte noch keinen Menschen lebendig gelassen, der ihm unter die Tatzen gekommen war.
sentences.l: But she thought with that she wanted to be rid of the little tailor, for the bear had let no person live yet who had come under his paws.
sentences.i: But her thought was that this would rid her of the little tailor, for the bear had never yet left a soul alive who came under his paws.
sentences.n: los werden, “to become rid of,” takes an accusative object in German. lebendig lassen is “to leave alive.” unter die Tatzen kommen is the phrase for falling into a beast’s power.

sentences.t: Das Schneiderlein ließ sich nicht abschrecken, war ganz vergnügt, und sprach „frisch gewagt, ist halb gewonnen.“
sentences.l: The little tailor did not let itself be scared off, was quite content, and spoke “boldly ventured is half won.”
sentences.i: The little tailor would not be scared off; he was in the best of spirits, and said, “a thing boldly begun is half won.”
sentences.n: The proverb frisch gewagt ist halb gewonnen has no verb of being in its first half — two past participles stand alone. frisch is not “fresh” here but “briskly, boldly.” The same proverb comes back in KHM 119, where seven Swabians say it to a hare.

sentences.t: Als nun der Abend kam, ward mein Schneiderlein hinunter zum Bären gebracht.
sentences.l: When now the evening came, my little tailor was brought down to the bear.
sentences.i: Now when evening came, my little tailor was taken down to the bear.
sentences.n: mein Schneiderlein is the narrator’s “my,” a familiar aside that shows whose side the telling is on rather than any possession. ward is the old past of werden and makes the passive here.

sentences.t: Der Bär wollt auch gleich auf den kleinen Kerl los und ihm mit seiner Tatze einen guten Willkommen geben.
sentences.l: The bear wanted also at once to be at the little fellow and to give him with his paw a good welcome.
sentences.i: The bear meant to be at the little fellow at once and give him a good welcome with his paw.
sentences.n: auf jemanden los is a movement with the verb left out — “[to make] at someone” — which German can do without the gehen. wollt is the spoken wollte. Willkommen counts as masculine here, as it often does in the older language.

sentences.t: „Sachte, sachte,“ sprach das Schneiderlein, „ich will dich schon zur Ruhe bringen.“
sentences.l: “Gently, gently,” spoke the little tailor, “I will bring you to rest right enough.”
sentences.i: “Easy, easy,” said the little tailor, “I shall quiet you soon enough.”
sentences.n: schon again in its soothing sense, “right enough, never fear.” zur Ruhe bringen is “to bring to quiet” — and the threat beneath the comfort is that it will also do for laying someone to rest.

sentences.t: Da holte es ganz gemächlich, als hätt es keine Sorgen, welsche Nüsse aus der Tasche, biß sie auf und aß die Kerne.
sentences.l: Then it took quite leisurely, as if it had no cares, walnuts out of its pocket, bit them open and ate the kernels.
sentences.i: Then, quite at his ease, as though he had not a care, he took walnuts out of his pocket, cracked them open and ate the kernels.
sentences.n: welsche Nüsse — literally “foreign nuts” — are walnuts; welsch meant Romance, Italian or French, and so anything come from the south. als hätt es keine Sorgen drops the wenn and puts the verb first. The es is still the neuter Schneiderlein.

sentences.t: Wie der Bär das sah, kriegte er Lust und wollte auch Nüsse haben.
sentences.l: When the bear saw that, he got a desire and wanted to have nuts too.
sentences.i: When the bear saw that, he took a fancy to them and wanted nuts as well.
sentences.n: Lust kriegen is to get an appetite for a thing; Lust is desire of any kind, and carries none of the narrowness of the English word it looks like.

sentences.t: Das Schneiderlein griff in die Tasche und reichte ihm eine Hand voll;
sentences.l: The little tailor reached into the pocket and handed him a hand full;
sentences.n: in die Tasche greifen takes the accusative because the hand travels into the pocket; the dative would leave it already inside. eine Hand voll is written as two words in 1857.

sentences.t: es waren aber keine Nüsse sondern Wackersteine.
sentences.l: but they were no nuts but cobblestones.
sentences.i: but they were no nuts at all — they were cobblestones.
sentences.n: es waren with a plural verb: the es is only a placeholder and the real subject follows. sondern is the “but” that corrects a preceding negative. Wackersteine are the smooth round stones of a stream bed or a paved road.

sentences.t: Der Bär steckte sie ins Maul, konnte aber nichts aufbringen, er mochte beißen wie er wollte.
sentences.l: The bear stuck them into his maw, but could bring nothing open, he might bite as he wanted.
sentences.i: The bear put them into his jaws, but could get nothing open, bite as he might.
sentences.n: Maul is the mouth of a beast; a person’s is a Mund. aufbringen here is “to get open,” a cousin of aufbeißen. mochte … wie er wollte is the old concessive turn, “try as he might.”

sentences.t: „Ei,“ dachte er, „was bist du für ein dummer Klotz! kannst nicht einmal die Nüsse aufbeißen“ und sprach zum Schneiderlein „mein, beiß mir die Nüsse auf.“
sentences.l: “Well now,” thought he, “what a stupid block you are! cannot even bite the nuts open” and spoke to the little tailor “do, bite the nuts open for me.”
sentences.i: “Well now,” he thought, “what a stupid lump you are — you cannot even crack the nuts,” and he said to the little tailor, “come, crack the nuts for me.”
sentences.n: The bear is scolding himself: the du is his own address to himself. Klotz is a block of wood, used of a person as English uses blockhead. mein is not the possessive here but an old coaxing particle, roughly “do, come now,” still alive in southern speech. beiß … auf is the imperative of aufbeißen, and mir is a dative of interest, “for me.”

sentences.t: „Da siehst du was du für ein Kerl bist,“ sprach das Schneiderlein, „hast so ein großes Maul und kannst die kleine Nuß nicht aufbeißen.“
sentences.l: “There you see what a fellow you are,” spoke the little tailor, “have such a great maw and cannot bite the little nut open.”
sentences.i: “There you see what sort of fellow you are,” said the little tailor: “such a great mouth, and you cannot crack the little nut.”
sentences.n: The subject is dropped in hast — spoken German leaves out du where it is plain who is meant. ein großes Maul haben also means to be a braggart, and the tailor is surely using both senses at once.

sentences.t: Da nahm es die Steine, war hurtig, steckte dafür eine Nuß in den Mund und knack, war sie entzwei.
sentences.l: Then it took the stones, was quick, stuck in their stead a nut into its mouth and crack, it was in two.
sentences.i: Then he took the stones back, was quick about it, slipped a nut into his mouth instead, and crack — it was in two.
sentences.n: dafür is “in place of that,” and the exchange is the whole trick. knack stands where a verb might, the sound doing the work of the deed. entzwei is “in two, asunder.”

sentences.t: „Ich muß das Ding noch einmal probieren,“ sprach der Bär, „wenn ichs so ansehe, ich mein ich müßts auch können.“
sentences.l: “I must try the thing once more,” spoke the bear, “when I look at it so, I think I would have to be able to do it too.”
sentences.i: “I must try the thing once more,” said the bear; “when I watch it like that, I fancy I could do it too.”
sentences.n: ansehen, “to look at,” is separable, the an at the end. ichs is ich es and müßts is müßte es; the tale writes speech as it sounds. ich mein is the short first person of meinen, without its -e.

sentences.t: Da gab ihm das Schneiderlein abermals Wackersteine, und der Bär arbeitete und biß aus allen Leibeskräften hinein.
sentences.l: Then the little tailor gave him cobblestones once again, and the bear worked and bit into them out of all his bodily strength.
sentences.i: Then the little tailor gave him cobblestones once more, and the bear laboured and bit into them with all the strength of his body.
sentences.n: abermals is the old “once again.” aus allen Leibeskräften is the set phrase for straining with the whole body. hinein points into the stones and closes the clause.

sentences.t: Aber du glaubst auch nicht daß er sie aufgebracht hat.
sentences.l: But you do not believe either that he got them open.
sentences.i: But you may be sure he never got them open.
sentences.n: The teller turns and speaks to you, the listener — a stroke of the spoken tale. It is a statement in form and a denial in force: “you will not believe he managed it,” meaning that he did not.

sentences.t: Wie das vorbei war, holte das Schneiderlein eine Violine unter dem Rock hervor und spielte sich ein Stückchen darauf.
sentences.l: When that was over, the little tailor fetched a violin forth from under its coat and played itself a little piece upon it.
sentences.i: When that was over, the little tailor brought a fiddle out from under his coat and played himself a little piece on it.
sentences.n: hervorholen, “to fetch forth,” is separable and hervor closes the clause. sich is a dative of interest — he plays for his own pleasure. Stückchen is the diminutive of Stück.

sentences.t: Als der Bär die Musik vernahm, konnte er es nicht lassen und fieng an zu tanzen,
sentences.l: When the bear perceived the music, he could not leave it and began to dance,
sentences.i: When the bear caught the music, he could not help himself and fell to dancing,
sentences.n: vernehmen is a graver word than hören — to catch or perceive a sound. es nicht lassen können is “to be unable to refrain.” fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing, and anfangen is separable: fieng … an.

sentences.t: und als er ein Weilchen getanzt hatte, gefiel ihm das Ding so wohl, daß er zum Schneiderlein sprach „hör, ist das Geigen schwer?“
sentences.l: and when he had danced a little while, the thing pleased him so well that he spoke to the little tailor “listen, is the fiddling hard?”
sentences.i: and when he had danced a while, the thing pleased him so well that he said to the little tailor, “tell me, is fiddling hard?”
sentences.n: gefallen runs the other way round from English “like”: the thing is the subject and the person stands in the dative — ihm gefiel das Ding, “the thing pleased him.” das Geigen is an infinitive used as a noun, “the fiddling.” daß is the 1857 spelling of dass.

sentences.t: „Kinderleicht, siehst du, mit der Linken leg ich die Finger auf und mit der Rechten streich ich mit dem Bogen drauf los, da gehts lustig, hopsasa, vivallalera!“
sentences.l: “Child’s-easy, you see, with the left I lay the fingers on and with the right I stroke away at it with the bow, then it goes merrily, hopsasa, vivallalera!”
sentences.i: “Easy as anything, you see: with the left hand I set the fingers on, and with the right I draw away at it with the bow, and then it goes merrily — hopsasa, vivallalera!”
sentences.n: kinderleicht is “as easy as for a child.” die Linke and die Rechte are the left and the right hand, with the noun left out. drauf los at the end of a verb means to set to it and keep at it. hopsasa and vivallalera are noises of merriment, not words to be construed.

sentences.t: „So Geigen,“ sprach der Bär, „das möcht ich auch verstehen, damit ich tanzen könnte, so oft ich Lust hätte.
sentences.l: “Such fiddling,” spoke the bear, “that I should like to understand too, so that I could dance as often as I had a mind.”
sentences.i: “Fiddling like that,” said the bear, “I should like to understand as well, so that I could dance whenever I had a mind to.
sentences.n: The object is named first and then picked up again by das, which throws the verb into second place and the subject after it. verstehen here is “to know how,” not merely “to understand.” damit is the conjunction “so that,” and könnte and hätte are the subjunctives of a thing wished for.

sentences.t: Was meinst du dazu?
sentences.l: What do you think to that?
sentences.i: What do you say to that?
sentences.n: meinen with dazu is to have an opinion on a thing. du is simply “you” — the tales use it between all who speak familiarly, and it carries no archaic colour.

sentences.t: Willst du mir Unterricht darin geben?“
sentences.l: Will you give me instruction in it?”
sentences.i: Will you give me lessons in it?”
sentences.n: darin is da + in, “in that,” standing where English says “in it.” wollen is “to want,” so the question asks the tailor’s willingness and is not a future.

sentences.t: „Von Herzen gern,“ sagte das Schneiderlein, „wenn du Geschick dazu hast.
sentences.l: “From the heart gladly,” said the little tailor, “if you have a knack for it.
sentences.i: “With all my heart,” said the little tailor, “if you have the knack for it.
sentences.n: von Herzen gern is the warm formula of consent. Geschick is aptitude, a hand for the thing.

sentences.t: Aber weis einmal deine Tatzen her, die sind gewaltig lang, ich muß dir die Nägel ein wenig abschneiden.“
sentences.l: But just show your paws here, they are mightily long, I must cut you the nails a little.”
sentences.i: But hold your paws out here a moment — they are mightily long; I must cut your claws a little.”
sentences.n: herweisen, “to show this way,” is separable and old-fashioned; weis is its imperative and has nothing to do with weismachen, to gull. einmal is not “once” but a softener, “just.” dir is the dative of the person concerned where English uses a possessive, “your nails,” and Nägel serves for a beast’s claws as well as a man’s nails.

sentences.t: Da ward ein Schraubstock herbei geholt, und der Bär legte seine Tatzen darauf,
sentences.l: Then a vice was fetched here, and the bear laid his paws upon it,
sentences.i: Then a vice was brought, and the bear laid his paws on it,
sentences.n: Schraubstock is the bench vice, from Schraube, a screw — the thing the whole trick turns on. herbeiholen is separable, and the 1857 text prints the halves apart.

sentences.t: das Schneiderlein aber schraubte sie fest und sprach „nun warte bis ich mit der Scheere komme,“ ließ den Bären brummen, so viel er wollte, legte sich in die Ecke auf ein Bund Stroh und schlief ein.
sentences.l: but the little tailor screwed them fast and spoke “now wait until I come with the scissors,” let the bear growl as much as he wanted, laid itself in the corner on a truss of straw and fell asleep.
sentences.i: but the little tailor screwed them tight and said, “now wait till I come with the shears,” let the bear growl as much as he liked, lay down in the corner on a truss of straw and fell asleep.
sentences.n: aber in second place is the tale’s way of turning to the other party. festschrauben and einschlafen are both separable. Scheere is the 1857 spelling of Schere, and ein Bund Stroh is a bundle or truss of straw.

sentences.t: Die Prinzessin, als sie am Abend den Bären so gewaltig brummen hörte, glaubte nicht anders, als er brummte vor Freuden und hätte dem Schneider den Garaus gemacht.
sentences.l: The princess, when she heard the bear growl so mightily in the evening, believed nothing other than that he growled for joy and had made an end of the tailor.
sentences.i: The princess, hearing the bear growl so mightily that evening, could believe nothing but that he was growling for joy and had made an end of the tailor.
sentences.n: nicht anders glauben, als … is “to believe nothing but that.” hören takes a bare infinitive: brummen hörte, “heard growl.” vor Freuden, “out of joy,” keeps an old plural, and jemandem den Garaus machen is the fixed phrase for finishing someone off. hätte is the subjunctive of what she supposed.

sentences.t: Am Morgen stand sie ganz unbesorgt und vergnügt auf, wie sie aber nach dem Stall guckt, so steht das Schneiderlein ganz munter davor und ist gesund wie ein Fisch im Wasser.
sentences.l: In the morning she got up quite untroubled and content, but when she looks toward the stable, there stands the little tailor quite brisk before it and is sound as a fish in the water.
sentences.i: In the morning she got up quite untroubled and pleased with herself; but when she looks towards the stable, there stands the little tailor before it, brisk as you please, and sound as a fish in water.
sentences.n: The tale slips out of the past into the present (guckt, steht, ist) at the moment of surprise, a common turn of spoken narration which the literal keeps. aufstehen is separable. gesund wie ein Fisch im Wasser is the German comparison where English says “fit as a fiddle”; the fish stays.

sentences.t: Da konnte sie nun kein Wort mehr dagegen sagen, weil sies öffentlich versprochen hatte,
sentences.l: Then she could now say no word more against it, because she had promised it publicly,
sentences.i: Now she could say not a word more against it, since she had given her promise publicly,
sentences.n: dagegen, “against it,” stands for the whole match. sies is sie es — a contraction the tale makes freely.

sentences.t: und der König ließ einen Wagen kommen, darin mußte sie mit dem Schneiderlein zur Kirche fahren, und sollte sie da vermählt werden.
sentences.l: and the king had a carriage come, in it she had to drive with the little tailor to church, and she was to be wedded there.
sentences.i: and the king had a carriage brought; in it she had to drive to church with the little tailor, and there she was to be married.
sentences.n: ließ … kommen is the causative again, “had a carriage come.” darin is da + in, “in which.” The last clause sets the verb before its subject (sollte sie) because it still hangs on the und before it.

sentences.t: Wie sie eingestiegen waren, giengen die beiden andern Schneider, die ein falsches Herz hatten und ihm sein Glück nicht gönnten, in den Stall und schraubten den Bären los.
sentences.l: When they had got in, the two other tailors, who had a false heart and did not grant him his luck, went into the stable and screwed the bear loose.
sentences.i: When they had got in, the two other tailors, who were false at heart and grudged him his good fortune, went into the stable and unscrewed the bear.
sentences.n: einsteigen, “to climb in,” takes sein for its perfect: waren eingestiegen. jemandem etwas gönnen is to allow another his good fortune without envy, so nicht gönnen is exactly “to grudge.” losschrauben is separable.

sentences.t: Der Bär in voller Wuth rannte hinter dem Wagen her.
sentences.l: The bear in full rage ran along behind the carriage.
sentences.i: The bear, in a full rage, came running after the carriage.
sentences.n: hinter … her marks pursuit, the her being a piece of hinterherrennen split across the clause. Wuth is the 1857 spelling of Wut.

sentences.t: Die Prinzessin hörte ihn schnauben und brummen:
sentences.l: The princess heard him snort and growl:
sentences.n: hören again with bare infinitives and no zu — snorting and growling are simply heard.

sentences.t: es ward ihr angst, und sie rief „ach, der Bär ist hinter uns und will dich holen.“
sentences.l: it grew fearful to her, and she cried “ah, the bear is behind us and wants to fetch you.”
sentences.i: fear came over her, and she cried, “ah, the bear is behind us and means to carry you off.”
sentences.n: es ward ihr angst is impersonal: the fear is not hers grammatically but befalls her, with ihr in the dative. holen is “to fetch,” and in a threat of this kind it means to carry off.

sentences.t: Das Schneiderlein war fix, stellte sich auf den Kopf, streckte die Beine zum Fenster hinaus und rief „siehst du den Schraubstock?
sentences.l: The little tailor was quick, set itself on its head, stretched its legs out at the window and cried “do you see the vice?
sentences.i: The little tailor was quick: he stood on his head, stuck his legs out of the window and cried, “do you see the vice?
sentences.n: fix is “quick, nimble,” and has nothing to do with being fixed. zum Fenster hinaus doubles the direction — out to the window and away — which German likes and English can only say once. The joke is that upside down his legs may pass for the vice.

sentences.t: wann du nicht gehst, so sollst du wieder hinein.“
sentences.l: if you do not go, then you shall [go] in again.”
sentences.i: if you do not be off, in you go again.”
sentences.n: wann is here the older spelling of wenn, “if.” The verb of motion is left out after sollst, so the literal supplies the bracketed “go,” which the 1857 text does not have — which German does freely when a direction word is present.

sentences.t: Wie der Bär das sah, drehte er um und lief fort.
sentences.l: When the bear saw that, he turned about and ran off.
sentences.n: umdrehen and fortlaufen are both separable, and both particles fall to the end of their clauses.

sentences.t: Mein Schneiderlein fuhr da ruhig in die Kirche und die Prinzessin ward ihm an die Hand getraut, und lebte er mit ihr vergnügt wie eine Heidlerche.
sentences.l: My little tailor drove then quietly to the church and the princess was wedded to his hand, and lived he with her content as a heath-lark.
sentences.i: My little tailor drove quietly on to church, and the princess was given him in marriage, and he lived with her as merrily as a lark.
sentences.n: jemandem an die Hand trauen is the old formula for giving a bride in marriage — her hand is laid in the bridegroom’s. The closing clause again sets the verb first, lebte er. vergnügt wie eine Heidlerche is the tale’s own comparison; the Heidlerche is the woodlark of the open heath.

sentences.t: Wers nicht glaubt, bezahlt einen Thaler.
sentences.l: Whoever does not believe it, pays a thaler.
sentences.i: Whoever does not believe it pays a thaler.
sentences.n: A closing formula of the spoken tale, half joke and half dare. Wers is wer es. The Thaler was a large silver coin, so the forfeit is a stiff one; the 1857 spelling keeps its h.

glossary.aufbringen: aufbringen — to get open (infinitive; here of cracking a shell, a cousin of aufbeißen)
glossary.bogen: der Bogen — bow (of a violin); also biegen — bent (past pl.)
glossary.bund: das Bund — bundle, truss (ein Bund Stroh: a truss of straw)
glossary.einmal: einmal — once; nicht einmal: not even; and after an imperative a softener, “just” (weis einmal her: just show)
glossary.fest: fest — firm, tight (adj./adv.; festhalten: to hold fast; fest glauben: to believe firmly)
glossary.gerathen: rathen — guessed (past part.; 1857 spelling of geraten; falsch gerathen: guessed wrong — not the geraten of landing in a place)
glossary.getraut: trauen — wedded, given in marriage (past part.; jemandem an die Hand trauen: to give a bride in marriage — not sich getrauen, “to dare”)
glossary.leg: auflegen — (I) lay on (1st sg. pres.; separable: leg … auf)
glossary.los: los — loose, rid of (los werden: to be rid of); also a particle — losschrauben: to screw loose; drauf los: away at it; auf jemanden los: at someone
glossary.mein: mein — my (poss.); also an old coaxing particle, roughly ‘do, come now’ (mein, beiß mir die Nüsse auf)
glossary.schon: schon — already; also the reassuring particle “right enough, never fear”
glossary.stich: der Stich — stitch (in sewing); also a prick, stab
glossary.streich: streichen — to draw, stroke (1st sg. pres.; mit dem Bogen streichen: to draw the bow across the strings)
glossary.wann: wann — if (here the older spelling of wenn; wann du nicht gehst: if you do not go)
glossary.weis: weisen — to show (imperative sg.; herweisen: to hold out, to show this way — not weismachen)
glossary.weiß: weiß — white (adj.); also wissen — to know (1st and 3rd sg. pres.: ich weiß, er weiß)
glossary.willkommen: der Willkommen — a welcome, a greeting (masculine noun in the older language; einen guten Willkommen geben)
glossary.wollt: wollen — wanted (3rd sg. past, clipped spoken form of wollte)
